recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation: No exploitable issue in this flow. In buyEntries (Raffle.sol:223-235), every state change happens before _safeMint: the USDC is pulled, totalEntries and ticketCount are updated, _ticketRanges is written and unsettledPot is increased. After the recipient hook returns, the function only emits TicketPurchased at line 236 and never reads ticket ownership again. In requestDraw, status, drawRequestedAt and vrfRequestId are all set before the native refund call at line 267, and nothing ticket-related runs after it. No guarded function reads ownerOf after an external call. redeemWinningTicket reads and burns the ticket (lines 320-325) before calling the prize contract. refundTickets reads ownership and burns tickets before its trusted USDC transfer. A ticket moved during the window therefore cannot desynchronize any later check. The only unguarded state-changing entry points are the ERC-721 transfer and approve functions. The _update override (line 497) screens every new owner. Nested calls into nonReentrant functions do revert and abort the outer call. However, only the party that started that call can trigger this: the buyEntries recipient is chosen by msg.sender, and the requestDraw refund goes to msg.sender. The whole transaction rolls back, including the USDC pull and the VRF request, so the only effect is that the caller's own attempt fails. No third party can block another user's purchase or the permissionless requestDraw. No randomness is known in either window, so selectively reverting cannot skew the draw. TicketPurchased.recipient is documented as the address that received the mint, and it did. Transfer events are emitted in the correct order. No on-chain code consumes this event, and the design says off-chain discovery is advisory.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation: No vulnerability in this flow. Calling refundTickets from inside the transfer hook is the same as recipient R refunding the ticket in a later transaction. (1) ERC721.safeTransferFrom (ERC721.sol:133-135) runs transferFrom to completion before it calls the hook. That means the auth check, the balance updates, _owners[id]=R and the previousOwner==from check (ERC721.sol:115-125) are all finished first. Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497-502) only adds a destination screen. So when R re-enters, the ownerOf check at Raffle.sol:359-360 reads real, final ownership, not a provisional value. (2) refundTickets burns each ticket (Raffle.sol:364) before it computes and pays the refund. A second refund of the same ID, whether a duplicate in the batch, a nested call or a later transaction, reverts in ownerOf with ERC721NonexistentToken. Ticket IDs are never reused because ticketCount only increases and minting needs Active status. (3) The payout is the ticket's stored range times ENTRY_PRICE. That is exactly what buyEntries added to unsettledPot (Raffle.sol:223-233), and enableRefunds copies that total into remainingRefundLiability (Raffle.sol:296-298). So the checked subtraction at Raffle.sol:368 always matches real outstanding liability; it cannot overpay or drift. (4) The only external calls inside refundTickets go to trusted contracts: the canonical USDC safeTransfer and the factory view calls in _isProtocolDestination. No untrusted code runs while the lock is held. Every value-moving function (refundTickets, redeemWinningTicket, the release* functions, enableRefunds, buyEntries, requestDraw) shares the same nonReentrant guard. (5) After the hook returns, safeTransferFrom only checks the returned selector and reads no other state. Ending with the ticket burned is consistent: Transfer from→R, then Transfer R→0, and balances net to zero. If R reverts, everything reverts, including the refund. (6) The data argument is passed to R and never parsed by Raffle. An approved operator who routes a ticket to R gets nothing beyond the transfer power the approval already gives. There is no double refund, liability error, wrong payee or stale-state read.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation: No exploitable vulnerability in this flow. Raffle overrides only _update (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:497). That override screens protocol sinks, which are this raffle, the factory, USDC, the VRF wrapper, the prize token, the implementation and same-factory raffles, before OZ's auth check and ownership write. When a recipient refuses the ticket, ERC721Utils.checkOnERC721Received (ERC721Utils.sol:33-47) reverts: either with ERC721InvalidReceiver or by re-throwing the recipient's own revert bytes. Either way the whole safeTransferFrom reverts. Ownership, balances, the cleared approval and anything done by reentrant calls inside the hook are all rolled back, so `from` keeps the ticket and only loses the gas they chose to spend. The hook can reenter because safeTransferFrom is not nonReentrant, but this is safe. The hook only runs after super._update has finished all state writes, safeTransferFrom writes nothing afterwards, and every reentrant path rechecks state itself (redeemWinningTicket and refundTickets require msg.sender == ownerOf, settlement is ownership-agnostic, and status gates apply). The recipient, which already owns the ticket at that point, gains nothing beyond what it could do in a separate transaction. Making a redemption conditional (redeem, then revert) gives no edge either, because the outcome is fixed on-chain and public: the winning entry is already set, and the prize or cash amount is deterministic. Inside buyEntries' _safeMint, the reentrancy guard is held, so the hook cannot call guarded functions. A foreign-factory raffle clone as recipient just reverts with UnexpectedPrize, so the ticket stays with `from`. The copy of unbounded revert data is standard OZ behaviour. It only burns gas in a transaction that reverts anyway, and it adds nothing over a recipient that simply burns its 63/64 gas allowance. Any harm would fall on an external wrapper that isn't part of this codebase. Recipients choosing whether to accept is required by EIP-721, so it is not a flaw.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation:
The described path works as written, but it is not a vulnerability. Only the winning ticket's owner, or an operator that owner approved, can start safeTransferFrom (ERC721.sol:115-124, _checkAuthorized). That caller already has full ERC-721 authority to send the ticket to any address. R becomes the real bearer at ERC721.sol:240, before the hook runs. Redeeming from onERC721Received therefore equals 'transfer to R, then R calls redeemWinningTicket', done atomically. Raffle.sol:23-26 and 491-492 say tickets are meant to be transferable bearer claims in every state.

Nothing is left inconsistent or open to double-claiming:
(1) ERC721.transferFrom finishes all state changes before checkOnERC721Received, and nothing runs after the hook except the selector check.
(2) redeemWinningTicket is nonReentrant. Before any external call it sets winnerRedeemed = true, burns the ticket, and sets prizeClaimed = true or zeroes winnerProceeds (Raffle.sol:323-341). Any nested redeem hits WinningTicketAlreadyRedeemed or the guard.
(3) Settlement inside the hook gives the same result no matter who calls it. unsettledPot is frozen once the status leaves Active. Ticket ranges never overlap, so only the real winning ticket passes _requireWinningTicket. Fee, cash and sponsor splits use exact 1e6 multiples and add up to grossPot.
(4) _update and _transferQuote still screen R against protocol sinks and raffle clones. NftWon and CashWon are terminal (enableRefunds only works from Active or Drawing), so releaseSponsorPrize cannot also release the NFT in NftWon.
(5) If R's hook, the prize delivery or the selector check reverts, the whole call frame reverts, including the redemption. Value cannot be kept while the transfer is undone.
(6) The untrusted prize contract cannot own tickets (rejected at Raffle.sol:498), and by the time it is called the winning ticket is already burned.

The outer safeTransferFrom finishing for a token that was burned in the same call is cosmetic. Transfer events and balances stay consistent. No unauthorized party gains the prize, and no liability is lost or double-paid.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation:
I found no concrete vulnerability in this flow. The recipient hook does run outside the reentrancy lock, but nothing it can do there breaks Raffle state.

1. All of OpenZeppelin ERC721._update's state writes finish before ERC721Utils.checkOnERC721Received calls the recipient (ERC721.sol:134-135). The authorization check, approval clearing, balance updates and `_owners[tokenId] = to` all run first. The Raffle._update override (Raffle.sol:497-502) only adds the protocol-destination screen. Raffle does not override safeTransferFrom or transferFrom, and nothing runs after the hook except the magic-value check. So there is no half-finished state to exploit and no later step that trusts stale ownership.

2. Raffle keeps no accounting tied to ownership or balances: no per-owner entry counters, snapshots or balanceOf reads. Ticket ranges (`_ticketRanges`) belong to the ticket ID, not the owner. The only functions that read ownership are redeemWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:320-321) and refundTickets (Raffle.sol:359-360). Both are nonReentrant, check `msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId)` when called, and burn the ticket before paying out.

3. If the recipient re-enters during the hook, it acts as the ticket's real current owner, with the owner's normal rights. Redeeming or refunding burns the ticket once and pays once:
   - Refund liability uses checked arithmetic (`remainingRefundLiability -= amount`).
   - Duplicate ticket IDs revert because ownerOf fails on a burned ticket.
   - `winnerRedeemed`, `prizeClaimed` and `settlementComplete` stop any second claim.
   Burning or moving the ticket inside the hook leaves ERC-721 balances consistent, because the outer `_update` has already finished.

4. The recipient cannot use the ticket temporarily and hand it back for a benefit that sticks. The only actions that use ownership burn the ticket, and if the hook returns a bad selector or reverts, the whole transaction rolls back atomically.

5. The `to` screen also applies to every nested transfer made during the hook. Raffle.sol:593-605 blocks these destinations, so a ticket cannot be moved into protocol plumbing:
   - the raffle itself
   - the factory
   - USDC
   - the VRF wrapper
   - the prize token
   - the raffle implementation
   - any registered sibling raffle

6. The other permissionless functions reachable from the hook have their own status and deadline checks, and none of them depends on the transfer in progress:
   - buyEntries
   - requestDraw
   - enableRefunds
   - settleWinningTicket
   - the release functions

7. The `data` bytes are passed through to the recipient only; Raffle never reads them. The caller pays the gas sent to their own chosen recipient. A ticket owner or approved operator gains no ability beyond what plain ERC-721 ownership already gives them.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation: No exploitable vulnerability was found in this flow. The Raffle._update override (Raffle.sol:497-502) runs _isProtocolDestination before super._update. That check compares `to` with the local sinks and then makes STATICCALLs to the immutable factory. raffleImplementation() is an immutable getter and isRaffle() is a mapping getter, so neither call can revert or be manipulated. Every registered clone is a CREATE-deployed minimal proxy that always has code: Raffle has no selfdestruct or arbitrary delegatecall. createRaffle registers the clone (RaffleFactory.sol:125) before any untrusted code runs (the prize safeTransferFrom at :128). Between Clones.clone (:106) and registration, the only external call is initialize, which makes only factory view calls. So the implementation and every existing sibling clone are always rejected. Three gaps remain: counterfactual future-clone addresses (the CREATE nonce is predictable), uninitialized clones of the implementation deployed by someone else, and clones from other factory deployments. Each only lets the ticket owner, or an operator they approved, strand that owner's own ticket. That is no different from sending it to any address with no key, and it needs no protocol flaw. No third party loses anything. Settlement is permissionless and storage-only, so it does not depend on who holds the ticket. Sponsor and treasury claims are independent of the ticket holder. Refunds of other tickets are unaffected. A clone that holds a foreign ticket can never move it, because a clone only calls its own prizeToken, and the factory requires the prize token to have code and rejects isRaffle[prizeToken]. The onERC721Received callback runs only after the ownership update has fully finished, and nothing is read after it, so reentry sees consistent state. The extra gas from the two view calls is not a security issue.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation:
No exploitable flaw in this flow. The ticket authorization boundary is the stock OpenZeppelin 5.6 ERC721 `_checkAuthorized`/`_isAuthorized` (ERC721.sol:164-187), and the vendored file's SHA-256 matches dependency-hashes.json. Raffle does not override `_isAuthorized`, `_checkAuthorized`, `_approve`, `_ownerOf`, `isApprovedForAll`, `getApproved`, `transferFrom`, `safeTransferFrom` or `_msgSender`. It never uses `_transfer` or `_safeTransfer`. Its only override, `_update` (Raffle.sol:497-502), runs a recipient screen and then passes `auth` (msg.sender) unchanged to `super._update`. That screen only makes view calls (STATICCALL) to the immutable trusted factory getters `raffleImplementation` and `isRaffle`. It does not change state or give anyone authority, so running it before the authorization check is harmless.

Unminted and burned tickets cannot be moved. Their `_owners` entry is 0. `_tokenApprovals` cannot be set because `approve` calls `_requireOwned`, and `_update`/`_burn` clear any approval. `_operatorApprovals[address(0)][*]` can never be true because `_setApprovalForAll` rejects a zero owner. So `_isAuthorized` is always false and the call reverts with ERC721NonexistentToken. A burned ID cannot be revived: ticket IDs come from the monotonically increasing `ticketCount` (checked `++`), so an ID is never minted twice. Tickets are burned only in `refundTickets` and `redeemWinningTicket`, and both first check that `msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId)`.

The ranges kept after a burn in `_ticketRanges` are only read by `refundTickets` (which needs ownership first) and `_settleWinningTicket`. Settlement is only possible in NftWon or CashWon, before any burn can happen in those states, and Refunding is a terminal state, so the kept ranges grant no transfer or claim authority. The locked implementation is constructed in Refunding with `initialized = true`, so it never mints tickets. The recipient's `onERC721Received` callback runs only after ownership has fully changed, so re-entering `redeemWinningTicket` or `refundTickets` from it is the legitimate new owner acting. No third party can transfer, revive or redirect a ticket through this path.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation: The flow is safe as traced, and there is no supported vulnerability. safeTransferFrom(from, address(0), id) calls the 4-arg overload (ERC721.sol:129), which calls transferFrom at :134. transferFrom reverts with ERC721InvalidReceiver(address(0)) at ERC721.sol:116-117, before Raffle._update runs, so nothing changes. Raffle does not override transferFrom or either safeTransferFrom overload. No other public ERC721 function calls _update with to == 0. _mint also rejects the zero address, and Raffle never uses the internal _transfer or _safeTransfer. As a result, the zero-address exemption in Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:498) is reachable only from the two internal _burn calls. Both check the owner first: redeemWinningTicket at Raffle.sol:320-325 sets winnerRedeemed and winnerRecipient, and refundTickets at Raffle.sol:359-368 reduces remainingRefundLiability. The rest of the transfer path also holds up. The recipient check rejects the raffle itself, the factory, the implementation, USDC, the VRF wrapper, the prize token and any raffle registered with the same factory. OZ checks authorisation and clears the approval. The untrusted onERC721Received callback runs only after the transfer is fully applied, and every Raffle state-changing function is nonReentrant. Re-entering from the callback can only do what the new owner could already do. A holder can still throw a ticket away by sending it to a dead non-zero address, but that harms only the holder's own claim and gives no attacker an advantage.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation: The recipient veto is standard OpenZeppelin 5.6 ERC-721 behaviour, and the Raffle adds no exploitable state around it. The vendored OZ files match dependency-hashes.json. The Raffle._update override (Raffle.sol:497-502) only screens out protocol destinations and then calls super._update; nothing in safeTransferFrom runs after checkOnERC721Received. If `to` rejects the ticket, whether by wrong selector, empty revert, running out of gas, or a bubbled reason (ERC721Utils.sol:32-46), the whole transaction reverts. Ownership, balances and the cleared approval go back to their prior state, along with anything the callback did. If `to` accepts, it is the legitimate owner at callback time. Any redeem or refund it makes during the callback (both nonReentrant and owner-checked, Raffle.sol:309-372) is something it could do directly, and the state is consistent at that point. The only party that pays gas or suffers the veto is the owner or approved operator who picked `to`. The Raffle never pushes tickets to untrusted recipients on its own paths. The only one is _safeMint to the buyer's chosen recipient in buyEntries, after all state updates and under nonReentrant. Refunds and redemption burn tickets, prize delivery uses plain transferFrom, and USDC goes out through SafeERC20 (Raffle.sol:235, 334, 404, 566). So a rejecting recipient cannot block settlement, refunds, sponsor or treasury releases, or other users. Copying a large revert payload only costs the caller who chose the recipient. Rejection by contracts and 7702-delegated EOAs is a usability limit, and transferFrom remains available. No third-party loss, fund lock or bypass of protocol invariants is reachable.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation: No vulnerability found in this flow. The rejection path behaves as intended and gives an attacker nothing to exploit. OZ v5.6 ERC721.safeTransferFrom(from,to,id) calls safeTransferFrom(...,"") (ERC721.sol:128-134), then transferFrom (:115-121), then the Raffle._update override. Every ERC-721 ownership change in OZ v5 passes through _update: mint, transfer, safe transfer and burn. Raffle overrides it and checks _isProtocolDestination(to, address(prizeToken)) before super._update (Raffle.sol:497-501), so there is no bypass. Burns pass to == 0, which skips the check, so redemption and refunds cannot be blocked by it. In _isProtocolDestination (Raffle.sol:598-604), the || chain first compares to against address(this), the immutable factory, the immutable quoteToken, the immutable i_vrfV2PlusWrapper (Chainlink base, immutable) and the stored prizeToken. A match short-circuits before the STATICCALL to factory.raffleImplementation(), and the later isRaffle query is skipped. The revert at :499 therefore happens before _checkAuthorized, before any balance or owner write, and before ERC721Utils.checkOnERC721Received. No state changes, and no untrusted recipient code runs. Raffle.onERC721Received cannot be reached with the raffle's own ticket, because to == address(this) is rejected first. Other clones from the same factory are rejected through isRaffle; the factory registers each clone before the untrusted prize transfer (RaffleFactory.sol:125-128), so the sponsor-controlled prize contract has no window. The factory also forbids raffles and the implementation as prize tokens. Checking the revert before authorization only changes which error an unauthorized caller sees. The remaining edge cases, such as sending a ticket to a code-less future clone address or to an unrelated contract, only strand the sender's own ticket. An approved operator could already do the same by sending to any burn address. No other party's funds, prize, settlement or payouts are affected. This leaves no realistic attacker-triggered harm on the configured production path.
